title: Parents as a door
hookLine: the parent is the middle door of the garden (Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: an old photo: dad and a brother he never mentions. what happened?

lines: THE MIDDLE DOOR OF THE GARDEN.
cards: Nine at night, and two plans collide. A parent's knee exercises need someone to count the reps, slowly. A group chat says the study session is starting.
Small choice. Hardly worth a thought. A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi calls it something bigger: a door.
The parent, it says, is the middle door of the garden of Paradise. Keep that door, or lose it. The word there is al-walid, the parent who gave you life.

teach.b: Why the middle door? Some readers say it's the best one, and the closest. You don't cross a desert to reach it.
It's down the hall. The Qur'an sets the tone for that hallway.
In Pickthall's words: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy." A bird lowering its wing over its young, turned around: now the grown child shelters the parent.
And it gives words to say with it: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." Then a scene. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ asking permission to go and fight.
The Prophet asked him: are your parents alive? Yes.
Then strive in their service. The great effort he went looking for was waiting at home. Another man asked who most deserved his good company.
Your mother, the Prophet said. Then who? Your mother.
Then who? Your mother. Then who?
So the door swings on two hinges. None of this asks anyone to stop living their own life. It asks what happens when two plans collide on a weeknight.
One for tonight: the man looking for the hardest striving was sent home to his parents.

how: Muslims call honoring parents birr al-walidayn, and say the Qur'an's prayer from 17:24, 'my Lord, have mercy on them both', for parents living or gone.

games.q: what does “parents as a door” mean?
o: obeying parents in every single thing they ask
serving your parents as a way to God's garden
a doorway in the house kept for the eldest

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: the middle door of the garden
the man who wanted to fight

s: serving parents only matters once they're old and sick
the man in the hadith had living, able parents: strive in their service, now.
in one hadith, the Prophet names the mother three times before the father
your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father.
the Qur'an gives words to pray for parents: have mercy on them both
17:24, 'as they did care for me when I was little.'

games.q: your mom calls during your game, for the third time today, with the same question about her phone. what fits 'lower the wing'?
o: let it ring; you've already explained it twice today.
answer kindly and walk her through it again.
answer, but tell her this is the last time.
games.why: the verse turns the bird's wing around: now the child shelters the parent, patiently, the way they once did for you.

practice: Count on your fingers the things a parent, or whoever raised you or looked out for you, did when you were small that you couldn't do for yourself. Meals, rides, nights up with a fever, a hand on the way to school.
If that relationship is hard, or they're gone, count what you honestly can. Some Muslims close with the Qur'an's words: my Lord, have mercy on them both.

wordCard.voice: Parents as a door: in the hadith, a parent is the middle door of the garden. Close by, and easy to walk past.

orig.note: Arabic: devotion to parents; the phrase Muslims use for honoring and serving them.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle door, just down the hall and open tonight. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1900 (Abu al-Darda': the parent is the middle of the gates of Paradise; keep that gate or lose it)

sources.q: lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy, and say: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3004 (a man asked to go and fight; are your parents alive? then strive in their service)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5971 (your mother, your mother, your mother, then your father)
